opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's changed a lot, honestly. A few years ago, I'd use these models mostly as a curiosity, almost like poking at them to see where they break. You'd ask something, and you'd double-check basically everything because the hallucination rate was just too high to rely on for anything serious.

Now it's quite different. I use them every day, for coding, for thinking through ideas, sometimes even for sanity-checking research directions. And I think the trust has grown in a very gradual, almost unconscious way. You don't wake up one day and say, "Okay, I trust the model now." It's more that you stop verifying certain kinds of things because, over hundreds of interactions, it just keeps being right. With boilerplate code or explaining a concept I half-remember, I mostly take the answer and move on.

But I think the interesting part is that the trust is very uneven. I trust it a lot on some things and not at all on others. On anything that's very recent, very niche, or where there's a precise number involved, I'm still pretty skeptical. And the tricky thing is that as models get better, the failure modes get more subtle. When a model was bad, the mistakes were obvious. When it's really good, the mistakes are buried inside something that looks completely plausible, so you almost need more vigilance in some sense, not less.

So I'd say my trust has gone up a lot overall, but it's become more calibrated rather than blind. It's a bit like working with a really strong colleague. You trust them, you delegate to them, but for the stuff that really matters, you still look over the work.

r001.rationale: The candidate says trust grew gradually and almost unconsciously as models improved and repeatedly proved reliable, leading him to stop checking some answers.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a funny one, because I think my trust has actually gone in a slightly weird direction. Early on, when models were obviously bad, I didn't trust them at all, and that was fine, because you'd never let them touch anything that mattered. You'd ask for a poem or a summary and you'd fact-check everything in your head anyway.

Now the models are genuinely useful. I use them every day for coding, for reading papers, for drafting things. And paradoxically, that's when trust becomes dangerous, because the failure modes got subtle. The model doesn't say something ridiculous anymore. It says something that's 95 percent right and sounds exactly like the 100 percent right version. So I've had to become more deliberate about where I verify. I trust them more on the stuff I can check cheaply, like code that has to compile or run against a test, and I trust them less on the stuff where being wrong is quiet, like a claim about a paper I haven't read or some number that gets pulled from nowhere.

The other thing is that having trained these models, I know too much about how the sausage is made. I know what the data looks like, I know where the evals are thin, I know how much of the apparent confidence is just a style the model picked up in post-training. That makes me a bit of a skeptic by default. But it also means I'm not surprised when it fails, and I think that's a healthier relationship than either blind faith or dismissing them. It's basically like working with a very fast, very well-read colleague who occasionally makes things up and never tells you when. You learn to design your workflow around that rather than hoping it stops happening.

r001.rationale: The candidate says usefulness makes trust more dangerous and requires deliberate verification; it does not describe trust becoming automatic.

astra-6.text:
I’d separate usefulness from trust. As models become more useful, I’m more willing to use them, but that doesn’t mean I’m equally willing to accept everything they say. You can have a model that helps you make progress very quickly and still need to check the important parts.

So the trust is conditional. If I can inspect the output, test it, or verify it, I’m comfortable giving the model more responsibility. If it’s answering something I don’t know enough about to evaluate, I’m much more cautious. Fluency makes it very easy to feel like you’ve gotten a good answer before you’ve actually established that it’s correct.

r001.rationale: The response says increased usefulness does not mean accepting everything models say and describes trust as conditional on being able to inspect or verify outputs. It does not describe trust becoming automatic as models improve.

sol-6.1.text: I think I trust them more as tools, but I’m still pretty careful about trusting what they say. As they become more useful, you use them for more things, and you get a better sense of where they work and where they fail. For coding, for example, I can look at the code, run it, and check the result. That makes it much easier to build trust. If I’m asking about something I don’t understand well enough to verify, I’m much more cautious. So usefulness has definitely gone up, but trust is still very task-dependent.
